messages.content: Write a post about starting a mentorship program on an engineering team. Around 250 words.

**We started a mentorship program. Here's what I'd do differently.**

Six months ago three of our juniors were quietly stuck. Not failing — shipping, passing review, showing up. Just not improving, and nobody had noticed because their PRs looked fine.

So we paired each of them with a senior engineer. Thirty minutes a week, on the calendar, non-negotiable.

The first version flopped. We told the pairs to "meet and discuss growth," which produced eight weeks of polite status updates. Mentorship without an agenda decays into a second standup.

What fixed it was giving every pair one artifact to work on together. A design doc the mentee was drafting. A gnarly bug in a service they'd never touched. A promo packet, talked through out loud. Something with edges. The conversation stopped being about career trajectory in the abstract and started being about why this retry loop swallows the error.

Two other things mattered. We let people leave a match without explaining themselves — one pair had zero chemistry and both were too polite to say so for a month. And we asked the seniors what they wanted out of it, which surfaced that half of them saw mentoring as unpaid overhead until we made it count in their own reviews.

Results after two quarters: two of the three juniors now lead features end to end. The third moved to a different team, which I also count as a win.

The whole thing costs about two hours a week of senior time. We should have done it a year earlier.

**We ran a mentorship program for two quarters. Here's the honest version.**

Last spring I realized three of our juniors had plateaued. They weren't struggling. PRs merged, standups happened, nothing was on fire. They just weren't getting better, and because the output looked normal, nobody clocked it.

We matched each one with a senior. Half an hour a week, blocked on the calendar, not movable.

Round one was useless. The instruction was "meet and talk about growth," and what we got was two months of polite status reporting. Give a mentorship pair no agenda and it turns into a second standup.

The fix was concrete: every pair needed one real thing in front of them. A design doc in progress. A bug in a service the junior had never opened. A promo packet read aloud. Something with edges to grab. Once that happened, the conversation stopped orbiting "career growth" and landed on why this retry loop eats the error.

Two more lessons. First, people need permission to exit a match without justifying it. One pair had no chemistry at all and spent a month being too well-mannered to admit it. Second, ask the seniors what they're getting. That question exposed the fact that most of them read mentoring as unpaid extra work, right up until it started counting in their own reviews.

Where we landed: two of the three juniors now own features start to finish. The third transferred to another team, which I count as working too.

Total cost is roughly two senior-hours a week. My only regret is the twelve months we spent not doing it.
